entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Epic of Jangar is a traditional oral epic poem that holds significant cultural importance for the Mongolian and Kalmyk peoples, with its origins tracing back to the 17th century, although its exact date of creation remains unknown. This narrative embodies the values, history, and identity of the Kalmyk people, who migrated from Mongolia to the Volga region of Russia in the 17th century. The epic is centered around the heroic figure of Jangar, a warrior who embodies the virtues of bravery and loyalty, reflecting the collective ethos of the Mongolian nomadic lifestyle.

The narrative unfolds across various adventures and battles, with Jangar and his companions facing formidable foes and supernatural challenges. The poem not only integrates historical elements such as the cultural conflicts between the Mongols and their enemies but also serves as a repository of Kalmyk folklore, blending mythological themes with historical narratives. The oral tradition of recitation has allowed the epic to adapt and evolve, ensuring its relevance across generations while preserving the Kalmyk language and cultural heritage.

The legacy of the Epic of Jangar is profound, influencing not only the cultural landscape of the Kalmyk people but also resonating with broader themes of identity and resilience within the Mongolian cultural sphere. The epic has inspired various art forms, including literature, theater, and music, serving as a bridge for intercultural dialogues between different ethnic groups within the region. Its enduring presence in Kalmyk society highlights the importance of oral traditions in preserving cultural identity in the face of modernity.

As the Kalmyks continue to navigate their cultural identity in contemporary Russia, the Epic of Jangar stands as a testament to their historical journey and cultural richness. It is said that 'the tales of Jangar remind us that every warrior has a story, and every story shapes a people.'

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Epic of Jangar (Kalmyk: Жангр, Zhangar; Mongolian: Жангар, Jangar) is the heroic epic of the Kalmyk people — a Mongolian Buddhist people whose ancestors migrated from the Dzungaria (western Mongolia) region to the lower Volga steppe in the early 17th century — and one of the three great epics of the Mongolian world alongside the Epic of Manas (of the Kyrgyz) and the Epic of Gesar (of the Tibetan/Mongolian world). The Jangar epic centres on the hero Jangar Khan, the ideal ruler of the mythical paradise kingdom of Bumba (also called Bumba-ba), and his twelve paladins (baatyrs, 'heroes') — who together defend the perfect land against external enemies. The paradise of Bumba is characterised by eternal spring, eternal youth (its inhabitants are permanently twenty-five years old), and the absence of death, disease, and suffering — an ideal world whose beauty and perfection gives the heroes their motivation for endless martial devotion.

The Jangar was performed by specialist bards called Jangarch (or Jangarchi), who memorised and performed the epic's 12–25+ songs (different performers and regions had different collections of songs) in multi-day performances accompanied by the Mongolian lute (tovshur). The oral tradition was first recorded in Russian in the 18th century — Nisan Ubashi (a Kalmyk scholar) recorded part of it in 1804–1805, and the Russian scholar Alexander von Bergmann made the first complete Russian translation in 1866 — and the Kalmyk oral tradition was systematically collected by Russian and Kalmyk scholars in the 19th–20th centuries. The standard Soviet-era canonical text (1978, compiled by Basang Dordzhiev and other scholars) includes 25 songs.

The Jangar is the primary monument of Kalmyk national literature and cultural identity — the Kalmyk people, decimated in the 18th century and again in the Soviet era (the 1943 deportation of the entire Kalmyk people to Siberia by Stalin, killing approximately 40% of the population), have maintained the Jangar as the central expression of their cultural survival and national heritage.
